title: Chapter test: Getting Started
summary: Ten questions on why Rust exists, your first program and Cargo. You need 70% to pass; you can retry.

questions.q: A C program writes to `a[3]` of an array that has one element. What does the C standard say happens?
options: The compiler refuses to build the program.
The program always crashes immediately with a clear message.
The behavior is undefined: the program may do anything.
The array grows to four elements automatically.
hints: This is the four-line program from *Programming Rust*.
questions.explanation: It is **undefined behavior**: the standard places no requirements at all, so the program might crash, print nonsense or be exploited. A Rust program doing the same with a vector stops with a clear `index out of bounds` panic instead.

questions.q: If a Rust program compiles, it cannot contain any logic errors.
hints: What exactly does the compiler know about your intentions?
questions.explanation: False. Rust rules out undefined behavior (invalid memory use, data races), not mistakes in your logic. A program that adds where it should subtract still compiles.

questions.q: Which are Rust's three goals, as *Rust in Action* puts them?
hints: Two options describe things Rust specifically does *not* have.
questions.explanation: Safety, productivity and control. Rust has no garbage collector, and it is statically typed: types are checked at compile time.

options: An error: two `println!` calls are not allowed
hints: What does the `ln` in `println!` stand for?
questions.explanation: `println!` prints its text and then a new line, so each call prints one line. `main` runs automatically; you never call it yourself.

questions.q: Which line would fail to compile?
hints: Is `println` a function or a macro?
questions.explanation: `println!` is a macro and must be called with `!`. Without it Rust looks for a *function* called `println`, which does not exist. `main` taking no parameters is correct.

questions.q: Which tool installs Rust and updates it with the `update` subcommand?
questions.explanation: `rustup` installs the toolchain; `rustup update` upgrades it and `rustup doc` opens the offline documentation.

questions.q: Order a typical Cargo workflow for a brand-new program.
items: `cargo build --release` to make the final program
hints: You need a project before you can edit it, and you ship last.
questions.explanation: Create, edit, check often, run to try, and build with optimizations at the end.

questions.q: Where does Cargo expect your source files?
options: Anywhere, as long as it is listed in `Cargo.lock`
hints: `cargo new` created one folder besides `target/` appearing later.
questions.explanation: Source code goes in `src/`. The top folder holds `Cargo.toml`, README and license; `target/` holds build output.

questions.q: `cargo build --release` produces a faster program than `cargo build`, but takes longer to compile.
hints: What does the release profile turn on?
questions.explanation: True. The release profile enables optimizations: slower to compile, faster to run. Always measure performance with the release build.

options: A package of Rust code, such as your project or a library
hints: Dependencies are listed as crates in `Cargo.toml`.
questions.explanation: A **crate** is a package of Rust code. Your project is a crate, and the libraries listed under `[dependencies]` are crates too.
